items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}] defined by [MATH: f(x)=3x+1.] Let's prove that this function is surjective.

Content:
First, recall the definition of a surjection:

Content:
> A function [MATH: f: X\rightarrow Y] is a surjection if, for every element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y,] there is at least one element in [MATH: X] that maps to [MATH: y{:}]
> [MATH: \forall \, y \in Y, \, \exists \, x \in X, \: f(x)=y]

Content:
Therefore, in this case, the surjectivity of [MATH: f] means the following:

Content:
> For all [MATH: y \in \mathbb{R}] there exists [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: 3x+1=y.]

Content:
To prove this, we need to take an arbitrary [MATH: y \in Y] and show that we can always find at least one value of [MATH: x\in X] that is mapped to [MATH: y] under [MATH: f.]

Content:
> So, let [MATH: y \in \mathbb{R}.] Then, we have the following:
> [MATH: f(x)|= y; 3x + 1|= y; 3x|= y − 1; x|= (y − 1)/(3)]

Content:
So, if we wish to map to [MATH: y\in\mathbb R,] we simply select [MATH: x = \dfrac{y-1}{3}\in\mathbb R.] Note that
[MATH: f\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) = 3\cdot \left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) + 1 = y.]
We continue our proof as follows:

Content:
> So, for every [MATH: y\in \mathbb R,] we have
> [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) = y.]

Content:
Finally, we state the conclusion:

Content:
> Therefore, [MATH: f] is a surjection.

Content:
For clarity, let's restate our proposition and its proof.

sections.normalized_html:
First, recall the definition of a surjection:

A function [MATH: f: X\rightarrow Y] is a surjection if, for every element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y,] there exists an element in [MATH: X] that maps to [MATH: y{:}] [MATH: \forall \, y \in Y, \, \exists \, x \in X, \: f(x)=y]

The negation of this statement is [MATH: \exists \, y \in Y, \, \forall \, x \in X, \: f(x) \neq y.] So, we get the following:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample.

In other words, we need to show that there exists [MATH: y] such that [MATH: f(x) \neq y] for any possible [MATH: x.]

We simply need to find a value [MATH: y] that does not have a preimage.

As a counterexample, let's take [MATH: y=(1,0).] Notice that
[MATH: f(m)|= y; (m, 3m − 1)|= (1, 0)] Since two pairs are equal if and only if their respective components are equal, we obtain the system [MATH: {m = 1; 3m − 1 = 0] which has no solution.

Finally, we state the conclusion:

Hence, the pair [MATH: (1,0)] has no preimage in [MATH: \mathbb{Z}.] Therefore, [MATH: f] isn't a surjection.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}] defined by [MATH: f(x)=3x+1.] Let's prove that this function is surjective.

Content:
First, recall the definition of a surjection:

Content:
> A function [MATH: f: X\rightarrow Y] is a surjection if, for every element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y,] there is at least one element in [MATH: X] that maps to [MATH: y{:}]
> [MATH: \forall \, y \in Y, \, \exists \, x \in X, \: f(x)=y]

Content:
Therefore, in this case, the surjectivity of [MATH: f] means the following:

Content:
> For all [MATH: y \in \mathbb{R}] there exists [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: 3x+1=y.]

Content:
To prove this, we need to take an arbitrary [MATH: y \in Y] and show that we can always find at least one value of [MATH: x\in X] that is mapped to [MATH: y] under [MATH: f.]

Content:
> So, let [MATH: y \in \mathbb{R}.] Then, we have the following:
> [MATH: f(x)|= y; 3x + 1|= y; 3x|= y − 1; x|= (y − 1)/(3)]

Content:
So, if we wish to map to [MATH: y\in\mathbb R,] we simply select [MATH: x = \dfrac{y-1}{3}\in\mathbb R.] Note that
[MATH: f\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) = 3\cdot \left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) + 1 = y.]
We continue our proof as follows:

Content:
> So, for every [MATH: y\in \mathbb R,] we have
> [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) = y.]

Content:
Finally, we state the conclusion:

Content:
> Therefore, [MATH: f] is a surjection.

Content:
For clarity, let's restate our proposition and its proof.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Restating the Full Proof

Content:
Proposition:

Content:
> The function [MATH: f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},] defined by [MATH: f(x)=3x+1,] is surjective.

Content:
Proof:

Content:
> A function [MATH: f: X\rightarrow Y] is a surjection if, for every element [MATH: y] in [MATH: Y,] there is at least one element in [MATH: X] that maps to [MATH: y{:}]
> [MATH: \forall \, y \in Y, \, \exists \, x \in X, \: f(x)=y]
>
> For all [MATH: y \in \mathbb{R}] there exists [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}] such that [MATH: 3x+1=y.]
>
> So, let [MATH: y \in \mathbb{R}.] Then, we have the following:
> [MATH: f(x)|= y; 3x + 1|= y; 3x|= y − 1; x|= (y − 1)/(3)]
>
> So, for every [MATH: y\in \mathbb R,] we have
> [MATH: f\left(\dfrac{y-1}{3}\right) = y.]
>
> Therefore, [MATH: f] is a surjection.
